 Telford Vice Share Tweet Bangladesh tour of South Africa, 2026 Riders of the storm will control Wanderers Test
 by Telford Vice •     Rickelton, who remained unbeaten on 56, called the day "pretty even" © AFP Rickelton, who remained unbeaten on 56, called the day "pretty even" © AFP A Joburg thunderstorm is a beautiful and wondrous thing; a fabulously pyrotechnic, fully electric, furiously hectic display of nature at its most forceful that reminds us mere and meek humans just how mere and meek we are. If you haven’t felt this power up close and personal you have not lived.
 Of course you might die if you’re in the wrong place at the right instant during a Joburg thunderstorm. Happily no-one died at the Wanderers on Tuesday. The storm that descended on the scene during Lunch on the third day of the first Test was determined to swamp the place with its superiority. First lightning, then rain, then hail amplified the point emphatically.
 The sky bristled with gnarled blue-black clouds and darkly muttered oaths long after play was called off 24 minutes after what would have been the end of the tea interval. More of the same — around twice as much, in fact — has been forecast for Wednesday. Those who only cricket know will grimace at that. The rest of us will look forward to it.
 All of us will appreciate that the match was exquisitely poised before the weather decided to raise hell. South Africa remain 14 runs behind with three wickets in hand. Ryan Rickelton, batted for more than two hours and faced 104 balls for his unbeaten 56, is key to the home side forging significantly past Bangladesh. Taking those three wickets quickly is how the visitors will stay in the game.
 That may not have been the case had South Africa not lost Wiaan Mulder, Marco Jansen and Simon Harmer for 15 runs in the space of 20 deliveries bowled with the second new ball. And, even more so, had Temba Bavuma not left the fray before any of those wickets had tumbled.
 He and Rickelton had batted together for 99 minutes, sharing 76 off 145 deliveries, when the new ball entered the narrative three overs after it became due. An over before it was taken Bavuma was flat on the ground receiving treatment on his right calf. His left was already strapped. Soon his right was even more heavily swathed.
 Bavuma rose, lowered the bottom half of his trouser leg, strapped his pad back into place and seemed ready to continue. But, a dozen deliveries later — all of them faced by Rickelton, who hit a four, a single, a two and another single; a decent enough fitness test — Bavuma tucked his bat under his arm and headed for the dressing room.
 Enter Mulder, Jansen and Harmer. And soon they exited, all in the wake of playing at wide deliveries from Taskin Ahmed and Hasan Mahmud, and all of them caught behind.
 At a press conference Rickelton rued the impact of Bavuma’s withdrawal: “It was unfortunately timed; on the doorstep of the new ball and exposing a new batter. It would have been ideal if he could have hung in there for another 10 overs to take the shine off.”
 What was the problem? And, more importantly, would Bavuma return?
 “I think it was cramp, maybe a bit of tightness. But I am aware he will be coming back to bat before the end of the innings.”
 Asked to summarise the 28 overs, Rickelton said, “The day was pretty even. We lost a few wickets with the new ball, which was unnecessary.”
 Then asked about his use of the last word in the above sentence, Rickelton walked it back: “I was being a bit harsh. Unfortunate is probably the right word. Like I said, it was unfortunate that Temba went off on the brink of the new ball and exposed new batters to the new ball. It can happen — it’s the new ball at the Wanderers; there are bound to be wickets.”
 Rickelton will have to forgive those who think he got it right the first time: it was significantly more unnecessary than unfortunate that South Africa lost three wickets for spit to the new ball. Those strokes didn’t need to be played. But they were. Now what?
 “We need to try and get a lead first and then try and maximise, even if it takes two sessions,” Rickelton said. “Then the pitch will start staying low and bring the poles into play.
 “If we can get a 100-run lead and put some more wear and tear onto the pitch our seamers can pitch it up more, which will bring up-and-down [bounce into play] and put pressure on them.
 “The challenge is between the ears. Whoever wins the first hour tomorrow will dictate the structure of the rest of the game.”
 A storm this way comes. Maybe two: one from above and another “between the ears”.
